etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium.

definitions.definition: (countable) Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 25:
quote.text: Where noyse of armes, or vew of martiall guize / Might not reuiue desire of knightly exercize.

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “§178”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: an exercise of the eyes and memory

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) Activity intended to improve physical, or sometimes mental, strength and fitness.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: This new-comer was a man who in any company would have seemed striking. […] He was smooth-faced, and his fresh skin and well-developed figure bespoke the man in good physical condition through active exercise, yet well content with the world's apportionment.

quote.citation: 2018, Timothy R. Jennings, The Aging Brain, →ISBN, page 107:
quote.text: Regular mental exercise keeps the circuits of the brain active and healthy and reduces the risk of dementia.

definitions.definition: A setting in action or practicing; employment in the proper mode of activity; exertion; application; use.

quote.citation: December 8, 1801, Thomas Jefferson, first annual message
quote.text: exercise of the important function confided by the constitution to the legislature

quote.citation: 1847, Alfred Tennyson, “(please specify the page number, or |part=Prologue, I to VII, or conclusion)”, in The Princess: A Medley, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: O we will walk this world, / Yoked in all exercise of noble end.

definitions.definition: The performance of an office, ceremony, or duty.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Lewis […]  refused even those of the church of England […] the public exercise of their religion.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene vii]:
quote.text: He doth entreat your Grace, my noble lord, To visit him tomorrow or next day. To draw him from his holy exercise.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) That which gives practice; a trial; a test.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 77:
quote.text: But patience is more oft the exerciſe / Of Saints, the trial of thir fortitude,

definitions.definition: To exert for the sake of training or improvement; to practice in order to develop.
(intransitive) To perform physical activity for health or training.
(transitive) To use (a right, an option, etc.); to put into practice.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ezekiel 22:29:
quote.text: The people of the land haue vsed oppression, and exercised robbery, and haue vexed the poore and needie: yea, they haue oppressed the stranger wrongfully.

definitions.definition: (now often in passive) To occupy the attention and effort of; to task; to tax, especially in a painful or vexatious manner; harass; to vex; to worry or make anxious.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book II”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 88–89:
quote.text: Where pain of unextinguiſhable fire / Muſt exerciſe us without hope of end

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To set in action; to cause to act, move, or make exertion; to give employment to.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 24:16:
quote.text: And herein doe I exercise my selfe to haue alwayes a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.

quote.citation: 1914 November, Louis Joseph Vance, “An Outsider […]”, in Munsey’s Magazine, volume LIII, number II, New York, N.Y.: The Frank A[ndrew] Munsey Company, […], published 1915, →OCLC, chapter I (Anarchy), page 373, column 2:
quote.text: Little disappointed, then, she turned attention to "Chat of the Social World," gossip which exercised potent fascination upon the girl's intelligence.
